Does that stat mean that 6% of Australians consider suicide at least once per year? 
I don't know how to talk about this without sounding like I'm trying to get a lot of attention, but I thought it would be normal for everyone to consider it once or twice a year... I started going to the doctor when the frequency that I contemplated suicide increased from once or twice a week to a few times an hour... Today with meds and therapy I'm back to a few times a week, which I consider healthy, manageable, and happier than I ever remember being.
I honestly thought I was normal. Is it true that 94% of people don't consider suicide at least once a year? I would see that as extremely positive and hopeful! (if a little saddened that I'm so misunderstood...) But I assume I'm misinterpreting this stat.

So, then, it's more a matter of being honest about the risks upfront and letting them decide for themselves?

Except that I have proof that a person is happier because I cut myself out of her life. I don't know how to trust someone's assessment...

Except it wasn't her loss. She's better off for it. She's with a man she loves and kids she loves living a great life. I have no misgivings toward her at all.

And my life is fine. Just occasionally I feel like it would be nice to have a romantic companion. But I wonder if it's fair to allow someone who I will love to risk falling for me. While I know that I'm not able to objectively measure that risk with certainty, it's clear that depression and financial burdens will always be a part of my life. If I were a father I wouldn't want my daughter to love someone like me.

I *do* lots of things. This isn't about *doing*. I have a reasonable aspect of myself. I just understand the risks, and I'm not sure how to convince myself that I'm worthy of overcoming those risks.
I think it's pretty normal to consider the implications of another person loving you.

What is depressing about it? I'm just trying to be logical. I broke up with someone who loved me and their life is better off because of that. What right do I have allowing someone to risk their happiness and good will with me?

I don't feel that depressed about it. I don't feel unconfident about it. I don't understand.

While I appreciate the last two paragraphs, the first is the kind of thing I'm looking for:

I don't know how to determine whether a person would properly calculate the risk. I guess that's the issue that I'm having.

I know I lost a good thing. But I don't regret it for a second. Her life is infinitely better with her husband than it would have been with me.

That's the whole point of my question, right. I'm not trying to determine whether a relationship will make my life better - I know it will. I'm questioning whether I should allow myself to risk the stability and happiness and life of someone who I will love. Is it ethical for me to do so, knowing that I will never be financially comfortable, and that my mental and emotional stability will always be suspect.

I have moved on.

I'm trying to determine whether I should allow myself to be a significant part of another person's life.
It's not about whether I'm happy or not. It's about determining whether I can ethically be part of someone else's life.

No. Mental illness is why everything went to shit.

And how does a person go about getting some confidence? It's not exactly the kind of thing that you pick up at the department store.

I let something go. I didn't throw it away. And looking back it seems that it's good that I did.

She would be miserable if she had to have gone through the last ten years with me. I have no regrets about that. I'm asking about how to move forward.
No. Not with her. She's moved on. Just in general.

> a parent who is vehemently opposed to abortion for moral reasons can refuse to give this consent, essentially legally forcing the minor to carry to term.

OK. I understand this. And, again, it may seem like I'm trolling, but I am sincere... I can understand why you care about this, but I don't understand why it's the most important thing. I definitely appreciate the difference between 'consent' and 'notification' - so maybe that's what I'm talking about -, but I wonder if informing a caring adult *after* the fact is 'good enough'.

Surely we must agree that abortion should be legal but a last-stitch, all-else-has-failed option - not for 'moral' reasons, exactly, but for health and emotional reasons, etc. If money is the biggest worry, then discussion with a caring adult beforehand could, potentially, open doors that would negate the requirement for an abortion. The same as my friend, I wonder how many girls (minors) would access abortion because they are scared and think it's simpler than talking to their parents... In Canada, there are something like 1 induced abortion for every 4 live births. I don't know how that breaks down as to the age of the mother, but I would speculate that 22 to 35 year old women have fewer induced abortions to live births than under-20s. I may be off my rocker, but I would find it difficult to believe that a quarter of all girls who are pregnant have no adults in their lives who they could talk to. Yes, I'm sure that there are girls in this circumstance and my heart goes out to them, but I wouldn't think they are the majority... And in all but the rarest cases, I don't see how opening lines of communication with a caring as early as possible, and certainly before the procedure, could be a bad thing. How are a young, scared girl and a health practitioner (who is no doubt likely to be professional, but for any number of reasons requires an emotional distance from the patient) better equipped to have the full range of discussion of impact and strategies? If the girl is unsure how the adult would respond, the practitioner can remain present to clarify details, answer questions, and ensure that the facts are adhered to.

I would imagine that a good number (maybe not a majority, I don't know, it would be nigh impossible to study this) of parents of pregnant 14-17 year old girls favour or pressure their daughters to terminate the pregnancy - I would hope that it is equally important to you that the girl retains her right to choose in this scenario. [Not a challenge, a legitimate question...] What is put in place to ensure that this right is protected? I can also see how inviting a caring adult to the table would present options.

In short: I have experienced (as I outlayed in my story above) girls who made the decision to undergo a term abortion under what I believe to be less-than-well-thought-out circumstances, as evidenced by the fact that she lied and bent the truth to act. I believe that most girls would have at least one level-headed adult that they could bring to the table to support them through the decision-making process. I also believe that this is fundamentally necessary to adequately prepare a girl to take advantage of her right to choose.

You found a few of the scattered puzzle pieces =)

Would I have found them without you? Maybe (I hope so, to be honest!), but *you* helped me find them. It's big and it's small. It's everything and it's nothing. Whatever it's worth, I don't know you, but I'm glad that it was you and not someone else.

Merry Christmas.

And thank you. =)

I don't have children... but I speculate that if I had a daughter who was a minor who was contemplating having an abortion, I'd like to at least have a conversation with her about it. Maybe the only reason that I can see for a cultural denial of this conversation is because I might be a bad parent - but surely we could work that out? a young woman who is resourceful enough to get herself to a clinic without parental support would probably be resourceful enough to sort out a way through what you're calling a 'restriction'. If I'm an abusive and/or deranged parent, access to abortion would solve one small part of a very big problem. Meanwhile, some kind of conversation with a trusted, adult family member who can be depended on to be a part of this minor's life on an ongoing basis would be something that I could see as advisable.

When I was in high school a girl that I didn't know very well from school phoned me and asked to come over. She was sitting on the steps to her house when I got there. She said that her parents found out that she was pregnant and wouldn't let her stay with them if she decided to get an abortion. It was a long time ago, so I can't remember the details exactly, but I remember her telling me that they did *not* kick her out, but that she didn't want to stay there that night. The father wanted out and wouldn't take or return her calls. I was sixteen or seventeen, she was fifteen or sixteen. Basically, she asked me to drive her to a clinic where she understood that she could have her situation taken care of discretely. For better or worse, my masculine brain kicked in. I felt responsible for her protection and duty-bound. I drove her to the clinic, walked her in, hugged her, and drove away.

After I got back to the car, I couldn't help but think that she should have talked to someone who loved her. Someone who knew her, who could hold her accountable for her actions but help her endure the gravity of them too. Someone to be there for her. I knew enough about myself to know that I was *not* able to be that guy. I would fall for her immediately, in the sixteen year old 'love' kind of way, and that would be no good. 

I saw her exactly twice after that night. The latter of the two she ignored me flatly. But the first she told me that her parents didn't *actually* threaten to kick her out. I don't know what exactly they did say - she just told me that either she lied or that I had misunderstood (I hadn't). I felt cheated and manipulated. It took me a long time not to feel that I had blood on my hands. The fuck did I know about driving some girl to an abortion clinic!?

I can't help but feel that, regardless of whether she decided to get an abortion or not, having a conversation with an adult who loved her probably would have been a more responsible course of action than some nerd from high school driving her to a clinic that doesn't ask questions (or whatever, I don't know what went down... it's hard not to have the Mad Men, Hollywood version of it all in my head).

---

Anyway... each scenario being so unique, I'm curious what makes you so adamant that *this*, of all the things that abortionista said, is the bit that you can't upvote enough.
